candidates.title: Improvement to continuous first-come admission: define safe admission units before joining
candidates.proposal:
Mechanism: retain the accessible first-come line and continuous admission, but establish each party’s smallest safe admission unit at arrival. The source leaves unresolved what happens when several spaces open but the next household cannot enter together. Improvised splitting can separate dependent children; improvised bypassing can undermine arrival order.

Using the site map, mark an accessible waiting route outside emergency access. One attendant manages arrivals and records admission units on the tally sheet; the other counts entries and exits against the established occupancy limit. At the existing arrival conversation, ask which children must enter with which caregiver. Families may choose separate units only when each can enter safely and caregivers agree. Record their consecutive positions before anyone enters. Count everyone according to site policy.

Admit the oldest unit when enough spaces exist. Do not bypass it merely to fill a smaller opening. Explain that keeping dependent parties together may temporarily leave spaces unused. Children unable to stand can wait beside the accessible line with their position retained and direct notification when needed.

This requires writing materials, a clock or watch, a known occupancy limit and a workable accessible route. If a proposed unit exceeds capacity, offer voluntary subdivision into safe units; if that is impossible, do not separate the child from required support. Explain that admission cannot proceed under the current capacity rule. If no accessible route exists, pause admissions and seek an authorized site correction. Stop new joining before the queue obstructs emergency access; the arrival attendant explains the pause and reopens joining only when safe space returns.
candidates.experiment: The arrival attendant owns a short trial at each event, comparing this arrangement with ordinary accessible first-come admission under the same occupancy rule. Preserve pending order when changing practices. Record sampled waits, admissions, disputes, ten-minute workload ratings, party-separation corrections and minutes with spare capacity while the first unit waits. Include unresolved waits at the hour’s end. Stop subdivision immediately if caregiver agreement or safe supervision is unclear; retain the intact party’s position. Reject the added recording if ordinary practice already handles parties reliably, or if extra workload and unused capacity outweigh fewer disputes or unsafe splits. Two events establish feasibility only.

candidates.title: Voluntary turn completion prompted at entry
candidates.proposal:
Mechanism: use the admission conversation to establish a voluntary turn-completion norm: when other children are waiting, families are asked to finish their turn after a posted suggested duration. This targets prolonged occupancy through an explicit caregiver commitment at an existing contact point. It retains continuous first-come admission and avoids compulsory cohort clearances. Its effect depends on voluntary cooperation; it creates no guaranteed turnover or return time.

Before opening, use the site map to mark an accessible queue and protect emergency access. Choose a suggested duration consistent with existing site rules and post it on a removable sign: ‘When others are waiting, please finish your turn after about this long, then rejoin for another turn.’ State that safe entry and exit time does not count toward the suggested play duration. The entrance attendant briefly explains the request as families enter and asks caregivers to help make room. Families without a caregiver receive the same simple explanation; compliance is not an admission condition.

One attendant manages arrivals, preserves positions for children who need adjacent accessible waiting, and prevents overflow. The second controls occupancy and gives the entry prompt. Neither patrols individual families or abandons the entrance to enforce the suggestion. Necessary caregivers stay with children, and mobility needs never trigger a shorter turn or hurried exit.

Resources are the map, tally sheets, removable signs, writing materials and a clock or watch. Safe capacity and an accessible waiting route remain prerequisites. If visitors cannot reasonably track elapsed time, describe the request as finishing after a reasonable turn and treat precise timing effects as uncertain. If cooperation is weak, continue ordinary first-come admission without escalating to compulsory removal.
candidates.experiment: The entrance attendant owns two preannounced comparison blocks during each event’s peak hour: ordinary continuous admission and admission with the voluntary prompt, reversing order at the second event. Keep queue order unchanged. Sample arrival-to-entry waits and visit durations using anonymous tally identifiers; record admissions, disputes, prompt repetitions and ten-minute workload ratings. Note demand and occupancy, including children still waiting at closing. Inspect emergency access throughout. Stop the prompt if it repeatedly delays entry control, produces arguments or pressures children needing longer transitions. A falsifying result is unchanged turnover and waiting combined with more staff work or disputes. Carryover between blocks and differences in demand limit conclusions; no improvement is assumed.
